blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 9 (Acid-Base Chemistry), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Explain how the Bronsted-Lowry concept removed the limitation of the Arrhenius theory. Using the reactions of HCl and NH₃ with water, show that water is amphoteric. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Limitation of Arrhenius theory: it describes the reaction of an acid and a base only in the aqueous medium, but many reactions occur in solvents other than water or with no solvent.

Bronsted-Lowry concept (1923, J.N. Bronsted and T.M. Lowry): acid-base reactions are proton-transfer reactions. An acid is the species donating a proton and a base is the species accepting the proton. Since no water or OH⁻ is required, it applies in any solvent and even without a solvent:
HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s)
HCl donates a proton (acid) and NH₃ accepts it (base), though no OH⁻ is present.

Water as a base: HCl(g) + H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
H⁺ from HCl attaches to a lone pair on the O atom of water; H₂O accepts the proton (base). Pairs: HCl-Cl⁻ and H₂O-H₃O⁺.

Water as an acid: NH₃(g) + H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
H⁺ from H₂O attaches to the lone pair on N; H₂O donates the proton (acid). Pairs: NH₃-NH₄⁺ and H₂O-OH⁻.

Since water acts as a base in one case and as an acid in the other, depending on the other reactant, it is amphoteric.

book_ref.quote: Bronsted-Lowry pointed out that acid–base reactions can be seen as proton-transfer reactions

blocks.prompt: 2 Define conjugate acid and conjugate base. For the reactions of HNO₃, H₂SO₄ and CO₃²⁻ with water given in Table 9.1, write each equation and name the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Conjugate acid: the species formed after a Bronsted base accepts a proton from the acid (e.g. H₃O⁺ is the conjugate acid of water).
Conjugate base: the species formed when an acid donates a proton to a base (e.g. Cl⁻ from HCl).

Equations:
HNO₃ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + NO₃⁻
H₂SO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + HSO₄⁻
H₂O + CO₃²⁻ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻

In each reaction the acid and its conjugate base differ by one proton, and the base and its conjugate acid differ by one proton (see table).

book_ref.quote: A species formed after a Bronsted base accepts a proton from the acid is called the conjugate acid.

blocks.prompt: 3 Define Lewis acids and bases. Explain the formation of acid-base adducts from (i) silver ion and ammonia (ii) boron trifluoride and fluoride ion, and show how the charge on each adduct is found. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Lewis concept (G.N. Lewis, 1923): acids and bases are identified by their ability to accept or donate a pair of electrons and form a coordinate covalent bond.
Lewis acid: any species (molecule or ion) that can accept a pair of electrons.
Lewis base: any species (molecule or ion) that can donate a pair of electrons.
A Lewis acid-base reaction occurs when a base donates a pair of electrons to an acid; the product is an acid-base adduct.

(i) Ag⁺ + 2NH₃ → [H₃N→Ag←NH₃]⁺
Each of the two NH₃ molecules (Lewis bases) donates its lone pair to the positively charged silver ion (Lewis acid). Sum of charges on the left = +1 + 0 + 0 = +1, so the adduct carries +1.

(ii) BF₃ + F⁻ → BF₄⁻
Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons in its valence shell (incomplete octet), so it is an electron pair acceptor, a very good Lewis acid. The fluoride ion (Lewis base) donates one of its lone pairs. Sum of charges on the left = 0 + (−1) = −1, so the adduct carries −1.

book_ref.quote: In the following reaction, each of two ammonia molecules, Lewis bases, donates a pair of electrons

blocks.prompt: 4 What is the ionic product of water? Derive its value at 25 °C and explain how it is affected by temperature and by adding a little acid or base. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Self-ionization: pure water is a poor but measurable conductor because it ionizes reversibly:
H₂O(ℓ) + H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq); net: H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Derivation: Kc = [H⁺][OH⁻]/[H₂O] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ mol dm⁻³
[H₂O] = 1000 g dm⁻³ ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 55.5 mol dm⁻³. Water is in large excess and very few molecules ionize, so [H₂O] is constant and is combined with Kc:
Kw = Kc[H₂O] = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ × 55.5 ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C
Kw is called the ionic product (dissociation constant) of water.

Neutral water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺]² = 10⁻¹⁴ and [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³.

Effect of temperature (Table 9.2): Kw increases with temperature: 0.11 × 10⁻¹⁴ (0 °C), 0.30 × 10⁻¹⁴ (10 °C), 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ (25 °C), 3.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ (40 °C).

Adding acid or base: with a little acid [H⁺] > [OH⁻]; with a few drops of base [OH⁻] > [H⁺]. [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are no longer equal, but Kw remains the same, 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.

book_ref.quote: Constant concentration of water is taken on L.H.S. and multiplied with Kc to get another constant called Kw.

blocks.prompt: 5 Using Table 9.2 (Kw = 0.11 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 0 °C and 3.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 40 °C), calculate [H⁺] and pH of pure water at 0 °C and at 40 °C. Is the water neutral at both temperatures? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺] = √Kw at each temperature; then pH = −log[H⁺].

book_ref.quote: The effect of temperature on Kw is shown in Table 9.2.

steps: At both temperatures [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so the water is neutral; only Kw (and so the pH of neutral water) changes with temperature
blocks.final_answer: 0 °C: [H⁺] = 3.3 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³, pH = 7.48; 40 °C: [H⁺] = 1.73 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, pH = 6.76; neutral at both

blocks.prompt: 6 Define pH and pOH. Why were these scales introduced? Show that pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C and find the pH and pOH of neutral water. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Need: in aqueous solutions the concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ are too low to be conveniently expressed and used in calculations. In 1909 Sørensen, a Danish biochemist, introduced the terms pH and pOH.

Definitions:
pH = −log[H⁺]
pOH = −log[OH⁻]

Relation: at 25 °C, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴. Taking −log of both sides:
−log[H⁺] + (−log[OH⁻]) = −log(10⁻¹⁴)
pH + pOH = 14

Neutral water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³
pH = −log(10⁻⁷) = 7 and pOH = −log(10⁻⁷) = 7

Range: the pH normally varies between 0 and 14 at 25 °C (pH < 7 acidic, pH > 7 basic, Figure 9.1), though solutions of negative pH and of pH above 14 are also known.

book_ref.quote: So, the scales of pH and pOH were developed.

blocks.prompt: 7 A solution has [H⁺] = 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ at 25 °C. Calculate its pH, pOH and [OH⁻] (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴), and state whether it is acidic or basic. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: pH comes straight from −log[H⁺]; pOH = 14 − pH; [OH⁻] from Kw/[H⁺].

book_ref.quote: Use the expression for Kw: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]

steps: pH < 7, so the solution is acidic

blocks.prompt: 8 The pH of a cleaning solution is 10.4 at 25 °C. Calculate its pOH, [H⁺] and [OH⁻]. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: pOH = 14 − pH; take antilogs: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ and [OH⁻] = 10⁻ᵖᴼᴴ (pH gives H⁺, pOH gives OH⁻).

book_ref.quote: Find the concentration of H⁺ and OH⁻, Taking antilog of pH and pOH

blocks.prompt: 9 What is the ionization constant Ka of an acid? Derive its expression for a weak acid HA, state its uses, and classify acids on the basis of Ka. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Many acids are weak electrolytes and ionize much less than 100%. The dissociation constant Ka is the quantitative measure of the strength of an acid.

Derivation: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻
Kc = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA][H₂O]
Water is in large excess, so its concentration is constant: Kc[H₂O] = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]
Let Kc[H₂O] = Ka. Hence Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] / [HA]

Uses:
1. Ka of any acid solution can be calculated if its pH (or [H⁺]) and the initial concentration of the acid are known.
2. The equilibrium [H₃O⁺] and [A⁻] can be calculated if the initial concentration of HA and its Ka are known.

Classification:
Ka < 10⁻³: weak acid (e.g. CH₃COOH, Ka = 1.85 × 10⁻⁵; H₂S, 1.0 × 10⁻⁷)
Ka = 1 to 10⁻³: moderately strong acid
Ka > 1: strong acid
The larger the Ka, the stronger the acid.

book_ref.quote: Suppose we have an acid HA dissolved in water,

blocks.prompt: 10 Show that the hydronium ion concentration of a weak acid HA of molar concentration C is given by [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka × C). State the assumption made. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Weak acids do not completely dissociate in water, so [H₃O⁺] is not equal to the initial concentration of the acid; the equilibrium expression is used.

Dissociation: HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)
In water: H⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq)
So: HA(aq) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq)

Let the initial concentration of HA be C mol dm⁻³. At equilibrium:
[H₃O⁺] = x, [A⁻] = x, [HA] = C − x

Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA] = (x × x)/(C − x) = x²/(C − x)

Assumption: for a weak acid x is very small compared to C, so C − x ≈ C:
Ka ≈ x²/C
Taking the square root: x ≈ √(Ka × C)
Thus [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka × C)

Example: for 0.1 mol dm⁻³ acetic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(1.8 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³.

book_ref.quote: The expression for the acid dissociation constant (Ka) is:

blocks.prompt: 11 Calculate [H₃O⁺], the pH and the percentage dissociation of a 0.20 mol dm⁻³ solution of acetic acid. (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Acetic acid is weak, so use [H₃O⁺] ≈ √(Ka × C); then pH = −log[H₃O⁺] and % dissociation = ([H₃O⁺]/C) × 100.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the concentration of [H₃O⁺] in a 0.1 M (mol dm⁻³) solution of acetic acid [CH₃COOH]

steps: CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺; C = 0.20 mol dm⁻³

blocks.prompt: 12 A 0.050 mol dm⁻³ solution of a weak monobasic acid HA has pH = 3.15. Calculate the Ka of the acid and classify it. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: From the pH find [H₃O⁺] = [A⁻]; the acid left is C − [H₃O⁺]; put these into Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA].

book_ref.quote: This equation can be used to calculate Ka for any acidic solution if we know the pH or [H⁺] of that solution

steps: Ka < 10⁻³, so HA is a weak acid

blocks.prompt: 13 Define the common ion effect. Explain it with the purification of sodium chloride by passing HCl gas through brine, giving the equilibrium equations. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Common ion effect: the suppression of ionization of a weak electrolyte by adding a common ion to it.

Purification of NaCl: brine is a saturated solution of NaCl, in which NaCl is fully ionized:
NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
Kc = [Na⁺][Cl⁻] / [NaCl]

HCl gas also ionizes in the solution:
HCl(g) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

Cl⁻ is the common ion. On passing HCl gas, the concentration of Cl⁻ increases. To maintain the constant value of the equilibrium constant, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ combine and NaCl crystallizes out:
Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → NaCl(s)

General result: the addition of a common ion to the solution of a less soluble electrolyte suppresses its ionization; the concentration of the unionized species increases and it may come out as a precipitate.

book_ref.quote: This type of effect is called the common ion effect.

blocks.prompt: 14 Explain with equations how the common ion effect is used in salt analysis (i) to obtain a low concentration of S²⁻ ions for the second group basic radicals (ii) to control [OH⁻] in the group reagent for the third group basic radicals. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Second group: H₂S is a weak acid:
H₂S(g) ⇌ 2H⁺(aq) + S²⁻(aq)
The stronger acid HCl is added: HCl(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
H⁺ is the common ion. It suppresses the dissociation of H₂S, which becomes less dissociated in acidic solution. In this way a low concentration of S²⁻ ions is produced, which helps to precipitate the second group basic radicals during salt analysis.

(ii) Third group: NH₃ solution gives OH⁻:
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
NH₄Cl is added; it is a strong electrolyte: NH₄Cl(aq) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
The large excess of the common ion NH₄⁺ suppresses the ionization of NH₃ solution, so the concentration of OH⁻ is lowered. The combination NH₄Cl + NH₃ (NH₄OH) is used as the group reagent for the third group basic radicals.

Thus the common ion effect finds extensive applications in qualitative analysis (and in preparing buffers).

book_ref.quote: This low concentration of S²⁻ ions helps to do the precipitation of radicals

blocks.prompt: 15 What are buffer solutions? How are acidic and basic buffers prepared? Explain how an acetic acid-sodium acetate buffer resists a change in pH. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Buffer solutions: solutions which resist the change in their pH when a small amount of an acid or a base is added to them. They have a specific constant pH which does not change on dilution or on keeping for a long time.

Preparation:
1. Acidic buffer (pH < 7): a weak acid + its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa.
2. Basic buffer (pH > 7): a weak base + its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH₄OH + NH₄Cl.

Action of acetic acid-sodium acetate buffer:
CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(ℓ) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
CH₃COONa(aq) → CH₃COO⁻(aq) + Na⁺(aq)
CH₃COOH is a weak electrolyte; CH₃COONa is a strong electrolyte whose CH₃COO⁻ suppresses the dissociation of CH₃COOH (common ion effect). So the buffer is a large reservoir of CH₃COOH and CH₃COO⁻.

On adding acid: the added H₃O⁺ ions react with CH₃COO⁻ to give back acetic acid, which, being a weak acid, prefers to remain undissociated:
CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ → CH₃COOH + H₂O
Hence the pH remains almost unchanged.

On adding base: the added OH⁻ ions react with the acid: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O, and the pH again remains almost unchanged. A NH₄Cl-NH₄OH buffer likewise resists the change of pH and pOH.

book_ref.quote: Buffer solutions are mostly prepared by mixing two substances.

blocks.prompt: 16 Write Henderson's equation for the pH of an acidic buffer. Which factors govern the pH of a buffer? Show that the best buffer has pH = pKa, and use Table 9.4 to explain the effect of adding acetate ions to acetic acid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Buffer of a weak acid HA and its salt NaA:
HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻;  NaA ⇌ Na⁺ + A⁻

Henderson's equation:
pH = pKa − log([Acid]/[Salt])
Interchanging numerator and denominator changes the sign of log:
pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid])

Factors: (i) the pKa of the acid used; (ii) the ratio of the concentrations of salt and acid.

Best buffer: prepared with equal concentrations of salt and acid. For acetic acid-sodium acetate, [CH₃COOH] = [CH₃COONa]:
pH = pKa + log(1) = pKa + 0 = pKa = 4.74
So the pH of such a buffer equals the pKa of the acid.

Table 9.4 (0.10 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH): as [CH₃COO⁻] rises 0.00 → 0.05 → 0.10 → 0.15 mol dm⁻³, the % dissociation falls 1.3 → 0.036 → 0.018 → 0.012 and the pH rises 2.89 → 4.44 → 4.74 → 4.92. The added acetate suppresses the dissociation of acetic acid; the greater [CH₃COOH] compared with [CH₃COONa], the lower the pH.

book_ref.quote: This equation shows that two factors evidently govern the pH of a buffer solution.

blocks.prompt: 17 A buffer is prepared with 0.25 mol dm⁻³ acetic acid and 0.10 mol dm⁻³ sodium acetate. Calculate its pH (pKa of acetic acid = 4.74). Is it an acidic or a basic buffer? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put the salt and acid concentrations into Henderson's equation pH = pKa + log([Salt]/[Acid]).

book_ref.quote: pH of a buffer solution can be calculated by using Henderson equation as given below:

steps: pH < 7: an acidic buffer (weak acid + its salt with a strong base)

blocks.prompt: 18 How many moles of sodium acetate must be dissolved in 1.0 dm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acetic acid to obtain a buffer of pH 5.04? (pKa = 4.74; assume no change in volume) (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rearrange Henderson's equation to find the ratio [Salt]/[Acid], then multiply by [Acid] and the volume.

book_ref.quote: So, pH is controlled by pKa of the acid.

steps: Moles of CH₃COONa = 0.20 mol dm⁻³ × 1.0 dm³ = 0.20 mol

blocks.prompt: 19 What is the solubility product? Derive the Ksp expression for PbSO₄, write it for PbCl₂, and state the general rule for writing Ksp. Use Table 9.6 to relate Ksp to solubility. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A soluble ionic compound like NaCl dissociates completely, but for a slightly soluble salt the dissociation is not complete at equilibrium. When PbSO₄ is shaken with water, the solution contains Pb²⁺, SO₄²⁻ and undissociated PbSO₄; equilibrium exists between the solid and its dissolved ions:
PbSO₄(s) ⇌ Pb²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)
Kc = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] / [PbSO₄]

Being sparingly soluble, the concentration of PbSO₄ almost remains constant, so it is taken with Kc:
Kc[PbSO₄] = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻]
Kc[PbSO₄] = Ksp, so Ksp = [Pb²⁺][SO₄²⁻] = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ at 25 °C

For PbCl₂ (PbCl₂ ⇌ Pb²⁺ + 2Cl⁻): Ksp = [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]²

Definition: the solubility product is the product of the concentrations of ions raised to an exponent equal to the coefficient in the balanced equation. Ksp is usually very small at room temperature, it is temperature dependent, and it is a measure of the dissociation of a sparingly soluble salt.

Relation to solubility (molar solubility S): for a 2-ion salt such as PbSO₄, Ksp = S² (S = 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³); for 3-ion salts such as Ca(OH)₂ or CaF₂, Ksp = S(2S)² = 4S³ (Ca(OH)₂: 6.5 × 10⁻⁶, S = 1.175 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³; CaF₂: 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹, S = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³).

book_ref.quote: It means that equilibrium exists between solid solute, PbSO₄ and the dissolved ions

blocks.prompt: 20 Explain how the solubility product is used to predict precipitation, illustrating with the CaSO₄ example. How does a common ion affect the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Predicting precipitation: the product of the ion concentrations actually present (the ionic product) is compared with Ksp:

Example: Ksp of CaSO₄ = 2 × 10⁻⁵. A 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ solution of Ca²⁺ is added to a 10⁻² mol dm⁻³ solution of SO₄²⁻ at 25 °C. After mixing (equal volumes):
[Ca²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 10⁻²/2 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³
Ionic product = (5.0 × 10⁻³)(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol² dm⁻⁶
2.5 × 10⁻⁵ > 2 × 10⁻⁵ (Ksp), so CaSO₄ precipitates out.

Common ion effect on solubility: the presence of a common ion decreases the solubility of a slightly soluble ionic compound. For a saturated solution of PbCrO₄ (PbCrO₄ ⇌ Pb²⁺ + CrO₄²⁻), a soluble salt that supplies CrO₄²⁻ makes CrO₄²⁻ combine with Pb²⁺ to form more insoluble PbCrO₄; the equilibrium shifts to the left to keep Ksp constant, so less PbCrO₄ stays dissolved.

book_ref.quote: The solubility product can also help in predicting whether the precipitation of a salt will occur or not.

blocks.prompt: 21 The solubility product of PbCl₂ at a certain temperature is 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ (value given). Calculate its molar solubility and the concentrations of Pb²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in its saturated solution. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Let the molar solubility be S; each PbCl₂ gives one Pb²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so Ksp = S(2S)² = 4S³.

book_ref.quote: Similarly, for another sparingly soluble salt, PbCl₂.

blocks.final_answer: S = 1.62 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³; [Pb²⁺] = 1.62 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³, [Cl⁻] = 3.24 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³

blocks.prompt: 22 At a certain temperature the molar solubility of Ca(OH)₂ is 1.05 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³. Calculate [Ca²⁺], [OH⁻] and the Ksp of Ca(OH)₂ at this temperature. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Each Ca(OH)₂ gives one Ca²⁺ and two OH⁻; put S and 2S into Ksp = [Ca²⁺][OH⁻]².

book_ref.quote: The concentration of OH⁻ is double than the concentration of Ca²⁺

blocks.prompt: 23 Predict whether a precipitate forms in each case (equal volumes are mixed): (i) a solution with 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ Pb²⁺ ions and a solution with 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ SO₄²⁻ ions (Ksp of PbSO₄ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁸) (ii) a solution with 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ Ag⁺ ions and a solution with 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ Cl⁻ ions (Ksp of AgCl = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration; compare the ionic product of the mixture with Ksp.

book_ref.quote: As the product of concentrations is greater than Ksp, therefore CaSO₄ will precipitate out.

steps: Ionic product = (2.0 × 10⁻³)(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol² dm⁻⁶ > 1.6 × 10⁻⁸, so PbSO₄ precipitates
Ionic product = (1.0 × 10⁻⁵)(1.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol² dm⁻⁶ < 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so the solution is unsaturated: no precipitate
blocks.final_answer: (i) PbSO₄ precipitates (2.0 × 10⁻⁶ > Ksp); (ii) no AgCl precipitate (1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ < Ksp)

blocks.prompt: 24 What is salt hydrolysis? Explain, with equations, the nature of aqueous solutions of the salts of (i) a strong acid and strong base (ii) a strong acid and weak base (iii) a weak acid and strong base (iv) a weak acid and weak base. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Salt hydrolysis: when a salt dissolves in water it dissociates into its ions; these ions can interact with water and affect the pH, depending on the acid and base from which the salt is derived.

(i) Strong acid + strong base, e.g. NaCl:
NaCl(s) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
Cl⁻ (conjugate base of strong HCl) and Na⁺ (conjugate acid of strong NaOH) are very weak and do not significantly react with water. The solution remains neutral.

(ii) Strong acid + weak base, e.g. NH₄Cl:
NH₄Cl(s) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺(aq)
NH₄⁺, the conjugate acid of weak NH₃, produces H₃O⁺; Cl⁻ does not react. The solution is acidic.

(iii) Weak acid + strong base, e.g. CH₃COONa:
CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
CH₃COO⁻, the conjugate base of weak CH₃COOH, produces OH⁻; Na⁺ does not affect the pH. The solution is basic.

(iv) Weak acid + weak base, e.g. NH₄CH₃COO:
NH₄CH₃COO(aq) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)
NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ and CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻
Both ions hydrolyze; the pH depends on their relative strengths. The solution may be acidic, basic or nearly neutral, depending on which reaction is more dominant.

book_ref.quote: When a salt dissolves in water, it dissociates into its constituent ions.

blocks.prompt: 25 What is an acid-base indicator? Explain the working of a weak-acid indicator HIn in acidic and basic solutions. State the criteria for selecting an indicator for a titration. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Indicator: a substance that changes colour to mark a titration's end point. Acid-base indicators show one colour in acid and another in base; most are weak organic acids or weak organic bases.

Weak-acid indicator: HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻
In⁻ is the anion part of the indicator. The reaction is reversible, so both HIn and In⁻ are present; the colours result from HIn and In⁻ having different colours.

In acidic solution: any In⁻ ions act as Bronsted bases and accept protons from the acid. The indicator is present largely in the unionized form HIn and shows the acid colour.

In basic solution: OH⁻ ions from the base combine with the H⁺ ions produced by the indicator. The indicator molecules ionize further to make up the loss of H⁺, so the indicator is present largely as In⁻ and shows the base colour (blue for litmus).

Indicator range: the colour depends on the relative amounts of HIn and In⁻ at a given pH; an indicator changes colour over about 2 pH units. Methyl red changes from red to yellow between pH 4.4 and 6.2 (mostly red HIn at pH 4.4).

Criteria for selection:
1. The pH at the end of the titration should be close to the indicator's neutral point (its colour-change range).
2. The indicator should show a sharp colour change near the equivalence point of the titration.

book_ref.quote: Acid-base indicators exhibit one color in acid and another in base.

blocks.prompt: 26 Describe the titration curve for the titration of aqueous ammonia with hydrochloric acid. Why is the pH at the equivalence point below 7, and which indicator is suitable? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Start: the solution contains only the weak base NH₃, which only partially dissociates, giving a lower [OH⁻] than a strong base. The initial pH is greater than 7 but lower than that of a strong base.

Adding HCl: as HCl is added, [OH⁻] decreases, causing a further decrease in pH.

Before the equivalence point: the solution is in a buffer-like region where the pH changes more gradually. The weak base and its conjugate acid NH₄⁺ (from the salt formed) create a buffering effect that moderates the pH change as the acid is added.

Equivalence point: the pH is less than 7 (pH = 5.27), because the conjugate acid slightly dissociates and releases H⁺ ions, making the solution acidic:
NH₄⁺ → NH₃ + H⁺

After the equivalence point: the pH decreases rapidly, because the excess strong acid dissociates completely and gives a high [H⁺].

Indicator: methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base, range 3.2-4.5) has its colour change in this acidic range, so it is used for strong acid-weak base titrations (Table 9.7).

book_ref.quote: Initially, the solution contains only the weak base and it only partially dissociates

blocks.prompt: 27 Define the equivalence point and the end point of a titration. How does a titration curve help in choosing an indicator? Illustrate with the strong acid-strong base titration and Table 9.7. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
pH curve: a graph of the pH of the solution versus the volume of titrant added; it shows how the pH of an acidic or basic solution changes as a basic or acidic solution is added.

Equivalence point: the point at which the amount of titrant added is just enough to neutralize the analyte solution completely.
End point: the point at which the indicator changes colour.

Choosing an indicator: the titration curve shows where the steep change of pH (the equivalence point) occurs. We choose an indicator whose end point (colour-change range) is close to the equivalence point.

Strong acid-strong base (HCl with NaOH): initially only the strong acid is present; it dissociates completely, so [H⁺] is high and the pH is very low. As NaOH is added, OH⁻ neutralizes H⁺ and the pH rises. The equivalence point is reached when the OH⁻ added is stoichiometrically equal to the H⁺ originally present; the pH there is 7.0. The curve shows a steep rise, the pH changing from about 4.0 to 10.0, so phenolphthalein, which shows different colours in this range, can be used.

Table 9.7:
Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in base, range 3.2-4.5; strong acid-strong base and strong acid-weak base titrations.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, red in base, range 8.2-10.0; weak acid-strong base titrations.

book_ref.quote: We can use the titration curve to choose an indicator that will show when the titration is complete
